newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians want new government to restore order.
newsitem.headline: Albanians want new government to restore order.

text.p: Albanians in the lawless south, hardest hit by unrest following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes and still ruled by armed gangs, eagerly await a new government to restore law and order.
The remnants of the police and army are powerless to stop gunmen robbing people and property and killing innocent bystanders in shootouts between rival gangs.

"There is an institutional vacuum because of the lack of an economic system and the total lack of institutions protecting law and order," said Ylli Asllani, mayor of the southern town of Gjirokaster, 230 km (140 miles) from Tirana.

Unrest in which at least 1,500 people were killed with weapons looted from army depots started in the south where the get-rich-quick schemes had gathered the life savings of Europe's poorest population.
Albanian border police said some 1,000 Albanians deported from neighbouring Greece this week fell prey to armed masked gangs after crossing the border.
A Greek businessman was kidnapped near Gjirokaster on Friday and his company has been asked to pay 50 million drachmas ($178,000) for his release.

"It's three weeks since the elections. What are they waiting for to create the proper structures of police and other institutions?" said Haxhi Demiri, police chief in the southern port of Vlore, 150 km (90 miles) from the capital.

Normal life in many southern towns lasts only until midday. People venture out to buy bread or fruit and vegetables, whose prices are high though no customs duty is being paid. Pensions and state salaries have not been paid for months.

"There is no police, prosecutor's office, court, banks, customs or taxation offices," said Kanan Zanaj, 65. "There are vigilantes and taxes are collected by armed masked men. Conflicts are resolved with Kalashnikovs."

The electoral commission announced final results of the June 29 parliamentary elections on Friday, raising hopes for an end to the standoff between Berisha and his Socialist opponents blocking formation of a new government.
Presidency sources said they expected Berisha to issue a decree on Saturday convening parliament for Monday.

A 7,000-strong multinational force deployed in April to accompany humanitarian aid and election monitors. They started leaving this week amid complaints that they had done nothing to restore law and order, though it was not within their mandate.

"The Italians patrolled only to use their diesel, nothing else," said Besmir Aliu, 58, in Vlore. "We want peace and quiet, elimination of the bands terrorising the town, because we are jailed in our homes."
"The Romanians did not even secure main roads, which was in their mandate," a policeman in Gjirokaster complained.

Berisha's Socialist party opponents and their coalition allies won a total of 117 seats in the 155-seat assembly. Berisha has said he will not cohabit with a Socialist government and will resign after convening the new parliament.
Mecan Bistri, a money dealer in Gjirokaster, said that Berisha should "soon leave his bunker-presidency office".
"If there are no obstacles for the new government it might repair everything," said pensioner Sanie Halimi, 64. "We are waiting for it to do something. That is why we voted for it."
The Socialists have promised they will continue market reforms and work towards Euro-Atlantic integration. They have also pledged there will be no sackings of state employees for political reasons.

Berisha's Democrats, who say they will boycott the first session of parliament in protest at the conditions in which the elections were held, are reviewing whether the party should rally behind the president or distance itself from him and find a new leader to improve its image.
